Title: 'Barbie' movie: Mattel's gross billings to rise by $125M thanks to film, CEO says
Text: [Barbie has dominated the summer box office grossing over $1.4B worldwide. One of the big beneficiaries has been the company that makes the toy, Mattel (MAT). Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz sat down with Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi to discuss all things Barbie, Mattel, and how the company has shifted in it's approach. According to Kreiz, gross billings, as a direct result of the Barbie movie, will increase by $125 million, at about a 60% operating income margin.Bigger picture, Kreiz explains the company's approach in “long-term franchise management” and how the company evolved from a toy manufacturing company to “an IP company that manages franchises”, using “cultural events to benefit the company for years to come." "It's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engage with your fans across multiple levels," Kreiz zays, adding that the opportunities are beyond just films.Click here for more of Yahoo Finance's coverage from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: Mattel chairman and CEO Ynon Kreiz. Ynon, where's-- Will Ferrell's behind you somewhere, right? I'm looking for him, no?YNON KREIZ: Great to see you, Brian. Thank you for having me.BRIAN SOZZI: So what is next on the Barbie front? We're starting to see every week the gross theater receipts continue to increase. You're approaching $2 billion. What is next for this franchise?YNON KREIZ: Well, we couldn't be more excited about the way the movie played out to resounding success, a real execution of Greta Gerwig's vision. And what we're seeing coming out of it, three things. It's the strength and cultural resonance of our brands, is our ability to attract, collaborate, and partner with top creative talent, and our ability to promote and create a cultural event of this movie, leveraging our commercial capabilities in partnership with Warner Brothers, who did a terrific job marketing the movie. So it's been a real combination driven by strong brand and great execution, both creatively and commercially.Story continuesBRIAN SOZZI: Your CFO gave a presentation earlier this morning, I think, for the first time, shared some numbers on how much Mattel may make from this movie. Can you share some of those numbers? And what does it mean for the future financial performance of the company?YNON KREIZ: Yes, we did talk about our revenue, gross billing this year to go up by about $125 million from movie, direct movie participation, toys, and consumer products directly related to the movie, not other Barbie product, at a 60%-- sorry, yeah, 60% operating income margin. So about $75 million operating income contribution directly related to the movie in 2023.BRIAN SOZZI: Is that higher than your expectations? Because from an outside looking in, that's a huge number. And in many respects, Ynon, that's a number that you didn't have last year on the financial statements.YNON KREIZ: Well, we did not expect the movie to be as successful. So it is more than we assumed entering the year. And we expect that in future years, there will be continued benefit from the movie. This is about long-term franchise management. It's not just about the quarter or the year.And we-- it's the thing that we've always talked about, you and me. This was the approach. It was never about just trying to sell more toys. It was about creating a cultural event, creating a societal moment. And we believe the benefit will carry forward for years to come.BRIAN SOZZI: We've talked a lot throughout the years. And this is the first time I've heard you mention franchise management. What does that mean as it pertains to now this cultural juggernaut that you've created? Of course, the Barbie brand has been there for decades. But now you have the movie, you have the content component. How do you manage this?YNON KREIZ: We started our journey as a toy company, as a toy manufacturing company. We evolved to be an IP company that manages franchises. And the biggest change in how we approach our business is to realize that people who buy our products and not just consumers, they are fans. And once you have a lot of fans, it's an audience.And when you realize that you have an audience, it changes the conversation. And the opportunity for you to continue to grow your business. And given that we own one of the strongest portfolios in children and family entertainment franchises in the world, this creates a very unique and exciting opportunities-- opportunity for us to grow outside of the toy aisle into highly accretive business verticals driven by big brands and big franchises, which we own. And the "Barbie" movie, we look-- we see as a template, as an example, in terms of how we approach franchise management and expect more to come.BRIAN SOZZI: You have a portfolio of really amazing toy brands that all of us in many respects have grown up using. How do you take this playbook and apply it to some of these brands? What will we see from Mattel over the next 24 months?YNON KREIZ: Our brands are very much timely as much as they are timeless. And we've been doing a lot of work around infusing cultural relevance and societal awareness for what we do with a very strong purpose behind our brands. So it's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engaging-- engage with your fans across multiple levels.And the opportunity for us is not just film. It's also television. It's video games. It's location-based entertainment. It's musicals. It's-- whatever medium is driven by big franchises and big brands. In today's world, this is what it's all about-- big brands, big franchises that elevate and rise above a crowded marketplace. And we believe we are at the beginning of a very exciting part of our journey.BRIAN SOZZI: Well, it's going to be hard to create another nearly $2 billion movie. It just doesn't happen very often. But within the portfolios that you and the portfolio brands you own, what's the brand you're really focused on that you're going to run this playbook with next?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. We're not saying every movie that we make will be as successful, but it will be the same approach, the same methodology, and the same creative take that we are looking to apply. There's the "Hot Wheels" movie that we're developing with JJ Abrams. There's a Matchbox movie with Skydance, which produced "Mission Impossible" and "Top Gun." There's a movie we're developing with Vin Diesel for Rock'em Sock'em Robots, Polly Pocket with Lena Dunham and Lily Collins, and Major Matt Mason with Tom Hanks written by Akiva Goldsman.So these are just a few examples of some of the projects that we're developing. And you can see, given the quality and strength and proven track record of our partners, we believe we have a real shot at creating exciting projects that will appeal to global audiences. And what we saw within the "Barbie" movie is that the picture appealed not just to the core buyers of Barbie toys, Barbie product, this was a much broader approach to global audiences across different demographics, men and women, different ages, different generations. And everyone found something that talked to them and touch them at an emotional level.And the credit goes to the incredible execution of this project by Greta Gerwig, who had such a vision and, of course, Margot Robbie as a producer and a lead actor, Ryan Gosling, and, of course, the soundtrack that was a key part of the holistic experience, all of it created something very special that we're very proud of.BRIAN SOZZI: This-- this didn't happen overnight. But my sense has been that you saw the potential of this happening many years ago when you took over at Mattel. From a leadership perspective, how did you identify that? And then how do you ultimately go about bringing that to life?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. This journey has been long in the making, started about five years ago. And from the very beginning, the approach was to create something that was not conventional, something that was not traditional. And the term "cultural event" is what we said back in the day. It was never about trying to make a movie or, for that matter, make a movie in order to sell toys.The focus was to create a quality content, quality content that people will want to watch. And we know that if we do that, and if we do that well, good things will happen. And we will sell a lot of toys. So it's not that we didn't want to sell toys, but the mandate and the approach and the relationship and the engagement with the creatives that partnered with us was to focus on making a great movie and not think about selling toys.And what we see now, of course, we have a great movie. We see the success at the box office. And we also are starting to see the success on the toy side of the company with POS for the company year-to-date up, Barbie gaining momentum. And overall, we see good, very exciting opportunity for us to continue to gain share.BRIAN SOZZI: Seemingly, every day, over the past three months, I've read another story about the "Barbie" movie, something new happening. But also, you, you've been front and center in a lot of these stories and on, as you should be, because you brought this to life, this cultural event. How have you stayed grounded? And how do you look-- how are you looking to stay grounded over the next few months when you have all these publications writing about you, telling you how successful you are? And how do you just stay focused with all this frenzy around yourself?YNON KREIZ: Well, this very much has been a team effort. It's been a journey with a lot of people that participated and made it all happen. And I couldn't be more proud of the team and everything that we've done collectively. For this to be successful, for this movie to be where it is today, it took a lot of effort. And I'm grateful for everyone's support and involvement.And we really do see it as a beginning of a new chapter. This is not a one-off movie. It's not a one-off project. This has been the strategy. And you followed our story, and you know that we've been consistently made progress in building and driving our IP strategy to reach this point.But it's not the moment we've been waiting to arrive, and we're done by any stretch. This is really one-- another step in the journey. We see it as a template. We see it as an example. As I said before, this is the approach. And we look to replicate that approach in terms of leveraging our brands that have been foundational in this case specifically-- you know, Barbie, it's the "Barbie" movie-- working with top talent that have a clear vision and are the best in what they do, which we have done in this movie as well. And of course, commercializing and executing the marketing level and creating demand in a marketplace that became a cultural phenomenon. And so this has been a great and exciting journey. And we're still very much at the early stage of it.BRIAN SOZZI: Thanks for making a little time for little old me and on. I appreciate it. I know you're the big star now. But I appreciate it. Thanks for always giving time to Yahoo Finance. It's been fun to follow this journey. I mean, hat tip to you and your team. Ynon Kreiz, Chairman and CEO of Mattel.Seana, back to you in New York. I know you're a big fan of the "Barbie" movie.SEANA SMITH: I am a big fan of the "Barbie" movie. We've been talking about it for over a year. So, of course, our thanks to you, saw all the great interviews out there, and Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz as well.]

Title: 'Barbie' movie soundtrack takes off on social media
Text: [The official soundtrack to Greta Gerwig's Barbie movie is finding similar success on social media and viral TikTok videos. Yahoo Finance's Alexandra Canal, Seana Smith, and Josh Schafer discuss the album, featuring songs from pop stars Dua Lipa, Nicki Minaj, and Charlie XCX, as its popularity has soared on this summer's trend of all things Barbie.Video TranscriptALEXANDRA CANAL: "Barbie," the phenomenon that is "Barbie," not only is the film outperforming, but their album is outperforming as well, debuting at number two on the Billboard 200, multiple singles. And I want to point out, too, that this was a global effort. There are global artists featured on this album. It was released through Warner Music so a holistic approach from Warner Brothers Discovery, which also produced the film.And I think TikTok, YouTube, that's been a big driver for the popularity of some of these songs, especially the newer ones like Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night." We also saw the resurgence of some older songs like Matchbox Twenty's "Push." And if you saw the movie, that was a scene that stuck with you. And that song was from the late '90s, so that making a resurgence as well. And I know that you did an experiment.JOSH SCHAFER: You guys have been hosting the show for the last hour and a half, I've been listening to the "Barbie" album.SEANA SMITH: It must be nice.JOSH SCHAFER: --doing a little market research.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Yeah.JOSH SCHAFER: Didn't love it.SEANA SMITH: Shocker. I was going to say, someone's been questioning "Barbie" ever since--JOSH SCHAFER: The same person that hasn't seen the movie, didn't love the album. But the one thing--ALEXANDRA CANAL: [INAUDIBLE].JOSH SCHAFER: Well, I like the Barbie girl song, the Nicki Minaj song. I think that one's good. I've heard that one on TikTok.ALEXANDRA CANAL: That's surprising.[INTERPOSING VOICES]JOSH SCHAFER: But I did you bring a trivia question, too, because I was curious about this. What do you guys think the most downloaded or I guess bought? Because it's going back to before we downloaded albums from a movie is, the most downloaded movie soundtrack, most purchased movie soundtrack. Any ideas?Story continuesALEXANDRA CANAL: I have no idea. I know like "Armageddon" makes me think of--SEANA SMITH: "Armageddon" is a good one.JOSH SCHAFER: Whitney Houston's "The Bodyguard." Because do you know what song was the headline of that?SEANA SMITH: One that got 45 million copies that were sold.JOSH SCHAFER: "I will Always Love You," Whitney Houston sings in that movie. But it did sort of remind me of what I like more about some movie soundtracks, which is when you have a very talented musical person, it makes for a really fun soundtrack, because you get a bunch of originals out of it. Think like "A Star is Born" with Lady Gaga. I really like that soundtrack more. That was the thing I didn't love about the "Barbie" soundtrack. There's a Ryan Gosling song on there, but it's not that good.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, but--JOSH SCHAFER: Like the actors weren't singers. So it's fun when the actors--SEANA SMITH: Ryan Gosling was a singer when he was younger.JOSH SCHAFER: He's not-- he's not Lady Gaga. He's not Lady Gaga.ALEXANDRA CANAL: No, but he was cute and funny. And that was the whole point of the movie, being cute.JOSH SCHAFER: Well, I haven't seen the movie. So I'm basing it off not seeing the movie.SEANA SMITH: But I think it also just speaks right to the fact that movies here can just play such a massive impact on the music industry in terms of sales, in terms of resurrecting some of those older songs, like you just said with Matchbox Twenty, and really even finding new stars. We've seen that happen time and time again with releases that have happened in the past and what that could mean for artists going forward.I have also not seen the movie yet. But I've heard a lot of these songs. A lot of them I've discovered via TikTok. So here we are in 2023 with the massive success, obviously, of TikTok. So many people finding these trends on that. And I think that also just unlocks future gains here for the music industry and movie tie-ups.JOSH SCHAFER: It gets to the music trend that we've talked about a lot, right, with the fact that you hear it now on TikTok. You and I both haven't even seen the movie, and I knew half the songs because I like, I could see them on TikTok. Right.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Right. I mean, I just remember "Dreams" a with the cranberry juice phenomenon. I'm a big Fleetwood Mac fan. And the fact that people are calling it that TikTok song really got me. But, hey, if that exposes it to a new generation, I'm all for it.SEANA SMITH: There we go. All right. Guys, we got to leave that there.]

Title: 'Equalizer 3' claims top box office spot over Labor Day Weekend
Text: [The third installment in Denzel Washington's Equalizer franchise took the top box office spot over the holiday weekend. Yahoo Finance Entertainment Reporter Alexandra Canal details the summer box office revenue after the premieres of the Barbie movie and Oppenheimer, while also commenting on Disney's (DIS) push to have streaming customers subscribe to Hulu's live-TV package.Video Transcript- Denzel Washington has made a return to the top spot at the box office this holiday weekend with the third installment of Equalizer, which is expected to wrap up the four day weekend at $42 million. That's according to Comscore. Now Barbie took the second spot with Blue Beetle, Gran Turismo, and Oppenheimer rounding out the top five. Yahoo Finance's Alexandra Canal joins us now with the details. Hey, Allie.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Hi, Rachelle. Yes. A solid Labor Day weekend at the box office, thanks in large part to the Equalizer 3. And Labor Day weekend, it hasn't historically been a holiday that draws people out to the theater. But this year seems to be a noteworthy exception. The film made $34.5 million in its opening weekend. And as you mentioned, is estimated to pull in 42 million over the four-day holiday weekend.And if we compare that to years past, that makes this year the second highest Labor Day weekend ever behind 2021. And remember, in 2021, we saw the debut of Marvel's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, which pulled in just under $100 million in that opening two years ago. So still a very strong start here, especially considering we don't have a Marvel film to save the box office this time around.And it's interesting to see the different types of movies that are outperforming at the box office this year. Obviously, The Equalizer. Huge star attached to that with Denzel Washington. An action movie. Typically, those are the movies that do well at the theater. However, this year, we're seeing different types of films emerge, like Barbie starring Margot Robbie. That was a huge success this summer. In fact, as the summer comes to a close the box office revenue hit $4 billion for the first time since the pandemic. So that's a huge win moving forward.Story continuesI will say there are certainly risks heading into the back half of this year. For example, Warner Brothers' Dune 2. That was pushed from November of this year to March of next year. And that was one of the most anticipated films of the fall. And the fact that we don't have that much content heading in to the back half of 2023 is concerning, especially amid these ongoing strikes in Hollywood. Dune 2 was pushed because of the strikes, and we could see potentially more reshuffling of the box office calendar as we head into the end of the year.So a lot to keep track of here, and certainly, the strikes are going to continue to have an impact. But so far at the box office, we're still seeing people come out to the theater, which is encouraging.- It's true. And even with a big name. I mean, look at Indiana Jones, that didn't do well. So I mean, it's kind of hit and miss for some of these as well. I also want to shift gears and look at the streaming space. Disney making a move to push users to subscribe to Hulu and its live TV offerings. What can you tell us there? That does seem like a like a reversal of fortunes here.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Yeah. So this follows the dispute that we saw late last week with Charter Communications, which is the parent company of Spectrum and Disney. If you remember last week, we had a lot of angry sports fans who were unable to watch the US Open, unable to watch college football. After Disney and Charter failed to reach an agreement, Disney then pulled all of its owned and operated channels from subscribers of Charter. So you weren't able to watch ABC, ESPN, even the Disney Channel. So that was very disappointing to those users.But now, Disney has an interesting tactic this morning, saying, if you're a subscriber to Charter and you're disappointed with all these blackouts, why don't you go and subscribe to Hulu Plus Live TV? So that's an interesting move to try and pump your own streaming offerings there. But we've heard from a lot of analysts that say Charter might be OK at the end of the day with this if a dispute is not resolved. However, this could have larger implications to the larger media space considering companies like Disney, Warner Brothers, Discovery, Paramount Global, they depend very heavily on the cash flow from linear networks.So if this sets a precedent moving forward, that could be devastating down the line. So this is something we're continuing to track and watch very closely since this feud, it's still ongoing at the moment.- We'll certainly be keeping track of that. It certainly does put front of mind all the streaming services available and just how much we're spending on them and then the streaming live TV options. It's a lot for us to have to deal with at the moment. But I know you'll keep us up to speed on all of it. Thank you so much, our very own Allie Canal.]

Title: Success of 'Barbie' movie could be financial boon for Mattel
Mattel CEO on Barbie movie: Here's how much we will make from the blockbuster in 2023
Text: [Mattel's (MAT) financial haul from the juggernaut Barbie movie is not all fun and games.It's real money — and a lot of it.Gross billings from Barbie, which include Mattel's cut of the movie box office and various merchandise, will be more than $125 million this year, Mattel chairman and CEO Ynon Kreiz told Yahoo Finance Live (video above) at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Tech Conference in San Francisco.The operating margin from these sales will be above a meaty 60%."It is more than we assumed entering the year, and we expect that in future years there will be continued benefit from the movie," Kreiz said.Mattel and Warner Bros. Discovery's "Barbie" has seen blockbuster success, bringing in over $1 billion worldwide.Mattel's "Barbie" live-action PG-13 flick, headlined by Margot Robbie as Barbie and Ryan Gosling as Ken, continues to clean up at the box office.More than a month into its theatrical release, Greta Gerwig’s blockbuster has hauled in a mind-blowing $1.4 billion-plus at the global box office.Mattel has positioned itself to win royally this coming holiday season from the eye-popping interest in all things Barbie.The toymaker has licensed the Barbie name to merchandise that is sprouting up everywhere.For instance, there is a Barbie apparel deal with specialty retailer Gap (GPS). The product line ranges from pink Barbie hoodies to pink pet clothing.A girl and her mother look at the window of the Zara store on Gran Vía street in Madrid with an advertising campaign for "Barbie". Title: 'Barbie' movie: Mattel's gross billings to rise by $125M thanks to film, CEO says
Text: [Barbie has dominated the summer box office grossing over $1.4B worldwide. One of the big beneficiaries has been the company that makes the toy, Mattel (MAT). Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz sat down with Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi to discuss all things Barbie, Mattel, and how the company has shifted in it's approach. According to Kreiz, gross billings, as a direct result of the Barbie movie, will increase by $125 million, at about a 60% operating income margin.Bigger picture, Kreiz explains the company's approach in “long-term franchise management” and how the company evolved from a toy manufacturing company to “an IP company that manages franchises”, using “cultural events to benefit the company for years to come." "It's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engage with your fans across multiple levels," Kreiz zays, adding that the opportunities are beyond just films.Click here for more of Yahoo Finance's coverage from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: Mattel chairman and CEO Ynon Kreiz. Ynon, where's-- Will Ferrell's behind you somewhere, right? I'm looking for him, no?YNON KREIZ: Great to see you, Brian. Thank you for having me.BRIAN SOZZI: So what is next on the Barbie front? We're starting to see every week the gross theater receipts continue to increase. You're approaching $2 billion. What is next for this franchise?YNON KREIZ: Well, we couldn't be more excited about the way the movie played out to resounding success, a real execution of Greta Gerwig's vision. And what we're seeing coming out of it, three things. It's the strength and cultural resonance of our brands, is our ability to attract, collaborate, and partner with top creative talent, and our ability to promote and create a cultural event of this movie, leveraging our commercial capabilities in partnership with Warner Brothers, who did a terrific job marketing the movie. So it's been a real combination driven by strong brand and great execution, both creatively and commercially.Story continuesBRIAN SOZZI: Your CFO gave a presentation earlier this morning, I think, for the first time, shared some numbers on how much Mattel may make from this movie. Can you share some of those numbers? And what does it mean for the future financial performance of the company?YNON KREIZ: Yes, we did talk about our revenue, gross billing this year to go up by about $125 million from movie, direct movie participation, toys, and consumer products directly related to the movie, not other Barbie product, at a 60%-- sorry, yeah, 60% operating income margin. So about $75 million operating income contribution directly related to the movie in 2023.BRIAN SOZZI: Is that higher than your expectations? Because from an outside looking in, that's a huge number. And in many respects, Ynon, that's a number that you didn't have last year on the financial statements.YNON KREIZ: Well, we did not expect the movie to be as successful. So it is more than we assumed entering the year. And we expect that in future years, there will be continued benefit from the movie. This is about long-term franchise management. It's not just about the quarter or the year.And we-- it's the thing that we've always talked about, you and me. This was the approach. It was never about just trying to sell more toys. It was about creating a cultural event, creating a societal moment. And we believe the benefit will carry forward for years to come.BRIAN SOZZI: We've talked a lot throughout the years. And this is the first time I've heard you mention franchise management. What does that mean as it pertains to now this cultural juggernaut that you've created? Of course, the Barbie brand has been there for decades. But now you have the movie, you have the content component. How do you manage this?YNON KREIZ: We started our journey as a toy company, as a toy manufacturing company. We evolved to be an IP company that manages franchises. And the biggest change in how we approach our business is to realize that people who buy our products and not just consumers, they are fans. And once you have a lot of fans, it's an audience.And when you realize that you have an audience, it changes the conversation. And the opportunity for you to continue to grow your business. And given that we own one of the strongest portfolios in children and family entertainment franchises in the world, this creates a very unique and exciting opportunities-- opportunity for us to grow outside of the toy aisle into highly accretive business verticals driven by big brands and big franchises, which we own. And the "Barbie" movie, we look-- we see as a template, as an example, in terms of how we approach franchise management and expect more to come.BRIAN SOZZI: You have a portfolio of really amazing toy brands that all of us in many respects have grown up using. How do you take this playbook and apply it to some of these brands? What will we see from Mattel over the next 24 months?YNON KREIZ: Our brands are very much timely as much as they are timeless. And we've been doing a lot of work around infusing cultural relevance and societal awareness for what we do with a very strong purpose behind our brands. So it's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engaging-- engage with your fans across multiple levels.And the opportunity for us is not just film. It's also television. It's video games. It's location-based entertainment. It's musicals. It's-- whatever medium is driven by big franchises and big brands. In today's world, this is what it's all about-- big brands, big franchises that elevate and rise above a crowded marketplace. And we believe we are at the beginning of a very exciting part of our journey.BRIAN SOZZI: Well, it's going to be hard to create another nearly $2 billion movie. It just doesn't happen very often. But within the portfolios that you and the portfolio brands you own, what's the brand you're really focused on that you're going to run this playbook with next?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. We're not saying every movie that we make will be as successful, but it will be the same approach, the same methodology, and the same creative take that we are looking to apply. There's the "Hot Wheels" movie that we're developing with JJ Abrams. There's a Matchbox movie with Skydance, which produced "Mission Impossible" and "Top Gun." There's a movie we're developing with Vin Diesel for Rock'em Sock'em Robots, Polly Pocket with Lena Dunham and Lily Collins, and Major Matt Mason with Tom Hanks written by Akiva Goldsman.So these are just a few examples of some of the projects that we're developing. And you can see, given the quality and strength and proven track record of our partners, we believe we have a real shot at creating exciting projects that will appeal to global audiences. And what we saw within the "Barbie" movie is that the picture appealed not just to the core buyers of Barbie toys, Barbie product, this was a much broader approach to global audiences across different demographics, men and women, different ages, different generations. And everyone found something that talked to them and touch them at an emotional level.And the credit goes to the incredible execution of this project by Greta Gerwig, who had such a vision and, of course, Margot Robbie as a producer and a lead actor, Ryan Gosling, and, of course, the soundtrack that was a key part of the holistic experience, all of it created something very special that we're very proud of.BRIAN SOZZI: This-- this didn't happen overnight. But my sense has been that you saw the potential of this happening many years ago when you took over at Mattel. From a leadership perspective, how did you identify that? And then how do you ultimately go about bringing that to life?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. This journey has been long in the making, started about five years ago. And from the very beginning, the approach was to create something that was not conventional, something that was not traditional. And the term "cultural event" is what we said back in the day. It was never about trying to make a movie or, for that matter, make a movie in order to sell toys.The focus was to create a quality content, quality content that people will want to watch. And we know that if we do that, and if we do that well, good things will happen. And we will sell a lot of toys. So it's not that we didn't want to sell toys, but the mandate and the approach and the relationship and the engagement with the creatives that partnered with us was to focus on making a great movie and not think about selling toys.And what we see now, of course, we have a great movie. We see the success at the box office. And we also are starting to see the success on the toy side of the company with POS for the company year-to-date up, Barbie gaining momentum. And overall, we see good, very exciting opportunity for us to continue to gain share.BRIAN SOZZI: Seemingly, every day, over the past three months, I've read another story about the "Barbie" movie, something new happening. But also, you, you've been front and center in a lot of these stories and on, as you should be, because you brought this to life, this cultural event. How have you stayed grounded? And how do you look-- how are you looking to stay grounded over the next few months when you have all these publications writing about you, telling you how successful you are? And how do you just stay focused with all this frenzy around yourself?YNON KREIZ: Well, this very much has been a team effort. It's been a journey with a lot of people that participated and made it all happen. And I couldn't be more proud of the team and everything that we've done collectively. For this to be successful, for this movie to be where it is today, it took a lot of effort. And I'm grateful for everyone's support and involvement.And we really do see it as a beginning of a new chapter. This is not a one-off movie. It's not a one-off project. This has been the strategy. And you followed our story, and you know that we've been consistently made progress in building and driving our IP strategy to reach this point.But it's not the moment we've been waiting to arrive, and we're done by any stretch. This is really one-- another step in the journey. We see it as a template. We see it as an example. As I said before, this is the approach. And we look to replicate that approach in terms of leveraging our brands that have been foundational in this case specifically-- you know, Barbie, it's the "Barbie" movie-- working with top talent that have a clear vision and are the best in what they do, which we have done in this movie as well. And of course, commercializing and executing the marketing level and creating demand in a marketplace that became a cultural phenomenon. And so this has been a great and exciting journey. And we're still very much at the early stage of it.BRIAN SOZZI: Thanks for making a little time for little old me and on. I appreciate it. I know you're the big star now. But I appreciate it. Thanks for always giving time to Yahoo Finance. It's been fun to follow this journey. I mean, hat tip to you and your team. Ynon Kreiz, Chairman and CEO of Mattel.Seana, back to you in New York. I know you're a big fan of the "Barbie" movie.SEANA SMITH: I am a big fan of the "Barbie" movie. We've been talking about it for over a year. So, of course, our thanks to you, saw all the great interviews out there, and Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz as well.]

Title: 'Barbie' movie soundtrack takes off on social media
Text: [The official soundtrack to Greta Gerwig's Barbie movie is finding similar success on social media and viral TikTok videos. Yahoo Finance's Alexandra Canal, Seana Smith, and Josh Schafer discuss the album, featuring songs from pop stars Dua Lipa, Nicki Minaj, and Charlie XCX, as its popularity has soared on this summer's trend of all things Barbie.Video TranscriptALEXANDRA CANAL: "Barbie," the phenomenon that is "Barbie," not only is the film outperforming, but their album is outperforming as well, debuting at number two on the Billboard 200, multiple singles. And I want to point out, too, that this was a global effort. There are global artists featured on this album. It was released through Warner Music so a holistic approach from Warner Brothers Discovery, which also produced the film.And I think TikTok, YouTube, that's been a big driver for the popularity of some of these songs, especially the newer ones like Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night." We also saw the resurgence of some older songs like Matchbox Twenty's "Push." And if you saw the movie, that was a scene that stuck with you. And that song was from the late '90s, so that making a resurgence as well. And I know that you did an experiment.JOSH SCHAFER: You guys have been hosting the show for the last hour and a half, I've been listening to the "Barbie" album.SEANA SMITH: It must be nice.JOSH SCHAFER: --doing a little market research.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Yeah.JOSH SCHAFER: Didn't love it.SEANA SMITH: Shocker. I was going to say, someone's been questioning "Barbie" ever since--JOSH SCHAFER: The same person that hasn't seen the movie, didn't love the album. But the one thing--ALEXANDRA CANAL: [INAUDIBLE].JOSH SCHAFER: Well, I like the Barbie girl song, the Nicki Minaj song. I think that one's good. I've heard that one on TikTok.ALEXANDRA CANAL: That's surprising.[INTERPOSING VOICES]JOSH SCHAFER: But I did you bring a trivia question, too, because I was curious about this. What do you guys think the most downloaded or I guess bought? Because it's going back to before we downloaded albums from a movie is, the most downloaded movie soundtrack, most purchased movie soundtrack. Any ideas?Story continuesALEXANDRA CANAL: I have no idea. I know like "Armageddon" makes me think of--SEANA SMITH: "Armageddon" is a good one.JOSH SCHAFER: Whitney Houston's "The Bodyguard." Because do you know what song was the headline of that?SEANA SMITH: One that got 45 million copies that were sold.JOSH SCHAFER: "I will Always Love You," Whitney Houston sings in that movie. But it did sort of remind me of what I like more about some movie soundtracks, which is when you have a very talented musical person, it makes for a really fun soundtrack, because you get a bunch of originals out of it. Think like "A Star is Born" with Lady Gaga. I really like that soundtrack more. That was the thing I didn't love about the "Barbie" soundtrack. There's a Ryan Gosling song on there, but it's not that good.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, but--JOSH SCHAFER: Like the actors weren't singers. So it's fun when the actors--SEANA SMITH: Ryan Gosling was a singer when he was younger.JOSH SCHAFER: He's not-- he's not Lady Gaga. He's not Lady Gaga.ALEXANDRA CANAL: No, but he was cute and funny. And that was the whole point of the movie, being cute.JOSH SCHAFER: Well, I haven't seen the movie. So I'm basing it off not seeing the movie.SEANA SMITH: But I think it also just speaks right to the fact that movies here can just play such a massive impact on the music industry in terms of sales, in terms of resurrecting some of those older songs, like you just said with Matchbox Twenty, and really even finding new stars. We've seen that happen time and time again with releases that have happened in the past and what that could mean for artists going forward.I have also not seen the movie yet. But I've heard a lot of these songs. A lot of them I've discovered via TikTok. So here we are in 2023 with the massive success, obviously, of TikTok. So many people finding these trends on that. And I think that also just unlocks future gains here for the music industry and movie tie-ups.JOSH SCHAFER: It gets to the music trend that we've talked about a lot, right, with the fact that you hear it now on TikTok. You and I both haven't even seen the movie, and I knew half the songs because I like, I could see them on TikTok. Right.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Right. I mean, I just remember "Dreams" a with the cranberry juice phenomenon. I'm a big Fleetwood Mac fan. And the fact that people are calling it that TikTok song really got me. But, hey, if that exposes it to a new generation, I'm all for it.SEANA SMITH: There we go. All right. Guys, we got to leave that there.]

Title: 'Equalizer 3' claims top box office spot over Labor Day Weekend
Text: [The third installment in Denzel Washington's Equalizer franchise took the top box office spot over the holiday weekend. Yahoo Finance Entertainment Reporter Alexandra Canal details the summer box office revenue after the premieres of the Barbie movie and Oppenheimer, while also commenting on Disney's (DIS) push to have streaming customers subscribe to Hulu's live-TV package.Video Transcript- Denzel Washington has made a return to the top spot at the box office this holiday weekend with the third installment of Equalizer, which is expected to wrap up the four day weekend at $42 million. That's according to Comscore. Now Barbie took the second spot with Blue Beetle, Gran Turismo, and Oppenheimer rounding out the top five. Yahoo Finance's Alexandra Canal joins us now with the details. Hey, Allie.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Hi, Rachelle. Yes. A solid Labor Day weekend at the box office, thanks in large part to the Equalizer 3. And Labor Day weekend, it hasn't historically been a holiday that draws people out to the theater. But this year seems to be a noteworthy exception. The film made $34.5 million in its opening weekend. And as you mentioned, is estimated to pull in 42 million over the four-day holiday weekend.And if we compare that to years past, that makes this year the second highest Labor Day weekend ever behind 2021. And remember, in 2021, we saw the debut of Marvel's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, which pulled in just under $100 million in that opening two years ago. So still a very strong start here, especially considering we don't have a Marvel film to save the box office this time around.And it's interesting to see the different types of movies that are outperforming at the box office this year. Obviously, The Equalizer. Huge star attached to that with Denzel Washington. An action movie. Typically, those are the movies that do well at the theater. However, this year, we're seeing different types of films emerge, like Barbie starring Margot Robbie. That was a huge success this summer. In fact, as the summer comes to a close the box office revenue hit $4 billion for the first time since the pandemic. So that's a huge win moving forward.Story continuesI will say there are certainly risks heading into the back half of this year. For example, Warner Brothers' Dune 2. That was pushed from November of this year to March of next year. And that was one of the most anticipated films of the fall. And the fact that we don't have that much content heading in to the back half of 2023 is concerning, especially amid these ongoing strikes in Hollywood. Dune 2 was pushed because of the strikes, and we could see potentially more reshuffling of the box office calendar as we head into the end of the year.So a lot to keep track of here, and certainly, the strikes are going to continue to have an impact. But so far at the box office, we're still seeing people come out to the theater, which is encouraging.- It's true. And even with a big name. I mean, look at Indiana Jones, that didn't do well. So I mean, it's kind of hit and miss for some of these as well. I also want to shift gears and look at the streaming space. Disney making a move to push users to subscribe to Hulu and its live TV offerings. What can you tell us there? That does seem like a like a reversal of fortunes here.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Yeah. So this follows the dispute that we saw late last week with Charter Communications, which is the parent company of Spectrum and Disney. If you remember last week, we had a lot of angry sports fans who were unable to watch the US Open, unable to watch college football. After Disney and Charter failed to reach an agreement, Disney then pulled all of its owned and operated channels from subscribers of Charter. So you weren't able to watch ABC, ESPN, even the Disney Channel. So that was very disappointing to those users.But now, Disney has an interesting tactic this morning, saying, if you're a subscriber to Charter and you're disappointed with all these blackouts, why don't you go and subscribe to Hulu Plus Live TV? So that's an interesting move to try and pump your own streaming offerings there. But we've heard from a lot of analysts that say Charter might be OK at the end of the day with this if a dispute is not resolved. However, this could have larger implications to the larger media space considering companies like Disney, Warner Brothers, Discovery, Paramount Global, they depend very heavily on the cash flow from linear networks.So if this sets a precedent moving forward, that could be devastating down the line. So this is something we're continuing to track and watch very closely since this feud, it's still ongoing at the moment.- We'll certainly be keeping track of that. It certainly does put front of mind all the streaming services available and just how much we're spending on them and then the streaming live TV options. It's a lot for us to have to deal with at the moment. But I know you'll keep us up to speed on all of it. Thank you so much, our very own Allie Canal.]

Title: Success of 'Barbie' movie could be financial boon for Mattel
Mattel CEO on Barbie movie: Here's how much we will make from the blockbuster in 2023
Text: [Mattel's (MAT) financial haul from the juggernaut Barbie movie is not all fun and games.It's real money — and a lot of it.Gross billings from Barbie, which include Mattel's cut of the movie box office and various merchandise, will be more than $125 million this year, Mattel chairman and CEO Ynon Kreiz told Yahoo Finance Live (video above) at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Tech Conference in San Francisco.The operating margin from these sales will be above a meaty 60%."It is more than we assumed entering the year, and we expect that in future years there will be continued benefit from the movie," Kreiz said.Mattel and Warner Bros. Title: 'Barbie' movie: Mattel's gross billings to rise by $125M thanks to film, CEO says
Text: [Barbie has dominated the summer box office grossing over $1.4B worldwide. One of the big beneficiaries has been the company that makes the toy, Mattel (MAT). Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz sat down with Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi to discuss all things Barbie, Mattel, and how the company has shifted in it's approach. According to Kreiz, gross billings, as a direct result of the Barbie movie, will increase by $125 million, at about a 60% operating income margin.Bigger picture, Kreiz explains the company's approach in “long-term franchise management” and how the company evolved from a toy manufacturing company to “an IP company that manages franchises”, using “cultural events to benefit the company for years to come." "It's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engage with your fans across multiple levels," Kreiz zays, adding that the opportunities are beyond just films.Click here for more of Yahoo Finance's coverage from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: Mattel chairman and CEO Ynon Kreiz. Ynon, where's-- Will Ferrell's behind you somewhere, right? I'm looking for him, no?YNON KREIZ: Great to see you, Brian. Thank you for having me.BRIAN SOZZI: So what is next on the Barbie front? We're starting to see every week the gross theater receipts continue to increase. You're approaching $2 billion. What is next for this franchise?YNON KREIZ: Well, we couldn't be more excited about the way the movie played out to resounding success, a real execution of Greta Gerwig's vision. And what we're seeing coming out of it, three things. It's the strength and cultural resonance of our brands, is our ability to attract, collaborate, and partner with top creative talent, and our ability to promote and create a cultural event of this movie, leveraging our commercial capabilities in partnership with Warner Brothers, who did a terrific job marketing the movie. So it's been a real combination driven by strong brand and great execution, both creatively and commercially.Story continuesBRIAN SOZZI: Your CFO gave a presentation earlier this morning, I think, for the first time, shared some numbers on how much Mattel may make from this movie. Can you share some of those numbers? And what does it mean for the future financial performance of the company?YNON KREIZ: Yes, we did talk about our revenue, gross billing this year to go up by about $125 million from movie, direct movie participation, toys, and consumer products directly related to the movie, not other Barbie product, at a 60%-- sorry, yeah, 60% operating income margin. So about $75 million operating income contribution directly related to the movie in 2023.BRIAN SOZZI: Is that higher than your expectations? Because from an outside looking in, that's a huge number. And in many respects, Ynon, that's a number that you didn't have last year on the financial statements.YNON KREIZ: Well, we did not expect the movie to be as successful. So it is more than we assumed entering the year. And we expect that in future years, there will be continued benefit from the movie. This is about long-term franchise management. It's not just about the quarter or the year.And we-- it's the thing that we've always talked about, you and me. This was the approach. It was never about just trying to sell more toys. It was about creating a cultural event, creating a societal moment. And we believe the benefit will carry forward for years to come.BRIAN SOZZI: We've talked a lot throughout the years. And this is the first time I've heard you mention franchise management. What does that mean as it pertains to now this cultural juggernaut that you've created? Of course, the Barbie brand has been there for decades. But now you have the movie, you have the content component. How do you manage this?YNON KREIZ: We started our journey as a toy company, as a toy manufacturing company. We evolved to be an IP company that manages franchises. And the biggest change in how we approach our business is to realize that people who buy our products and not just consumers, they are fans. And once you have a lot of fans, it's an audience.And when you realize that you have an audience, it changes the conversation. And the opportunity for you to continue to grow your business. And given that we own one of the strongest portfolios in children and family entertainment franchises in the world, this creates a very unique and exciting opportunities-- opportunity for us to grow outside of the toy aisle into highly accretive business verticals driven by big brands and big franchises, which we own. And the "Barbie" movie, we look-- we see as a template, as an example, in terms of how we approach franchise management and expect more to come.BRIAN SOZZI: You have a portfolio of really amazing toy brands that all of us in many respects have grown up using. How do you take this playbook and apply it to some of these brands? What will we see from Mattel over the next 24 months?YNON KREIZ: Our brands are very much timely as much as they are timeless. And we've been doing a lot of work around infusing cultural relevance and societal awareness for what we do with a very strong purpose behind our brands. So it's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engaging-- engage with your fans across multiple levels.And the opportunity for us is not just film. It's also television. It's video games. It's location-based entertainment. It's musicals. It's-- whatever medium is driven by big franchises and big brands. In today's world, this is what it's all about-- big brands, big franchises that elevate and rise above a crowded marketplace. And we believe we are at the beginning of a very exciting part of our journey.BRIAN SOZZI: Well, it's going to be hard to create another nearly $2 billion movie. It just doesn't happen very often. But within the portfolios that you and the portfolio brands you own, what's the brand you're really focused on that you're going to run this playbook with next?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. We're not saying every movie that we make will be as successful, but it will be the same approach, the same methodology, and the same creative take that we are looking to apply. There's the "Hot Wheels" movie that we're developing with JJ Abrams. There's a Matchbox movie with Skydance, which produced "Mission Impossible" and "Top Gun." There's a movie we're developing with Vin Diesel for Rock'em Sock'em Robots, Polly Pocket with Lena Dunham and Lily Collins, and Major Matt Mason with Tom Hanks written by Akiva Goldsman.So these are just a few examples of some of the projects that we're developing. And you can see, given the quality and strength and proven track record of our partners, we believe we have a real shot at creating exciting projects that will appeal to global audiences. And what we saw within the "Barbie" movie is that the picture appealed not just to the core buyers of Barbie toys, Barbie product, this was a much broader approach to global audiences across different demographics, men and women, different ages, different generations. And everyone found something that talked to them and touch them at an emotional level.And the credit goes to the incredible execution of this project by Greta Gerwig, who had such a vision and, of course, Margot Robbie as a producer and a lead actor, Ryan Gosling, and, of course, the soundtrack that was a key part of the holistic experience, all of it created something very special that we're very proud of.BRIAN SOZZI: This-- this didn't happen overnight. But my sense has been that you saw the potential of this happening many years ago when you took over at Mattel. From a leadership perspective, how did you identify that? And then how do you ultimately go about bringing that to life?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. This journey has been long in the making, started about five years ago. And from the very beginning, the approach was to create something that was not conventional, something that was not traditional. And the term "cultural event" is what we said back in the day. It was never about trying to make a movie or, for that matter, make a movie in order to sell toys.The focus was to create a quality content, quality content that people will want to watch. And we know that if we do that, and if we do that well, good things will happen. And we will sell a lot of toys. So it's not that we didn't want to sell toys, but the mandate and the approach and the relationship and the engagement with the creatives that partnered with us was to focus on making a great movie and not think about selling toys.And what we see now, of course, we have a great movie. We see the success at the box office. And we also are starting to see the success on the toy side of the company with POS for the company year-to-date up, Barbie gaining momentum. And overall, we see good, very exciting opportunity for us to continue to gain share.BRIAN SOZZI: Seemingly, every day, over the past three months, I've read another story about the "Barbie" movie, something new happening. But also, you, you've been front and center in a lot of these stories and on, as you should be, because you brought this to life, this cultural event. How have you stayed grounded? And how do you look-- how are you looking to stay grounded over the next few months when you have all these publications writing about you, telling you how successful you are? And how do you just stay focused with all this frenzy around yourself?YNON KREIZ: Well, this very much has been a team effort. It's been a journey with a lot of people that participated and made it all happen. And I couldn't be more proud of the team and everything that we've done collectively. For this to be successful, for this movie to be where it is today, it took a lot of effort. And I'm grateful for everyone's support and involvement.And we really do see it as a beginning of a new chapter. This is not a one-off movie. It's not a one-off project. This has been the strategy. And you followed our story, and you know that we've been consistently made progress in building and driving our IP strategy to reach this point.But it's not the moment we've been waiting to arrive, and we're done by any stretch. This is really one-- another step in the journey. We see it as a template. We see it as an example. As I said before, this is the approach. And we look to replicate that approach in terms of leveraging our brands that have been foundational in this case specifically-- you know, Barbie, it's the "Barbie" movie-- working with top talent that have a clear vision and are the best in what they do, which we have done in this movie as well. And of course, commercializing and executing the marketing level and creating demand in a marketplace that became a cultural phenomenon. And so this has been a great and exciting journey. And we're still very much at the early stage of it.BRIAN SOZZI: Thanks for making a little time for little old me and on. I appreciate it. I know you're the big star now. But I appreciate it. Thanks for always giving time to Yahoo Finance. It's been fun to follow this journey. I mean, hat tip to you and your team. Ynon Kreiz, Chairman and CEO of Mattel.Seana, back to you in New York. I know you're a big fan of the "Barbie" movie.SEANA SMITH: I am a big fan of the "Barbie" movie. We've been talking about it for over a year. So, of course, our thanks to you, saw all the great interviews out there, and Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz as well.]

Title: 'Barbie' movie soundtrack takes off on social media
Text: [The official soundtrack to Greta Gerwig's Barbie movie is finding similar success on social media and viral TikTok videos. Yahoo Finance's Alexandra Canal, Seana Smith, and Josh Schafer discuss the album, featuring songs from pop stars Dua Lipa, Nicki Minaj, and Charlie XCX, as its popularity has soared on this summer's trend of all things Barbie.Video TranscriptALEXANDRA CANAL: "Barbie," the phenomenon that is "Barbie," not only is the film outperforming, but their album is outperforming as well, debuting at number two on the Billboard 200, multiple singles. And I want to point out, too, that this was a global effort. There are global artists featured on this album. It was released through Warner Music so a holistic approach from Warner Brothers Discovery, which also produced the film.And I think TikTok, YouTube, that's been a big driver for the popularity of some of these songs, especially the newer ones like Dua Lipa's "Dance the Night." We also saw the resurgence of some older songs like Matchbox Twenty's "Push." And if you saw the movie, that was a scene that stuck with you. And that song was from the late '90s, so that making a resurgence as well. And I know that you did an experiment.JOSH SCHAFER: You guys have been hosting the show for the last hour and a half, I've been listening to the "Barbie" album.SEANA SMITH: It must be nice.JOSH SCHAFER: --doing a little market research.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Yeah.JOSH SCHAFER: Didn't love it.SEANA SMITH: Shocker. I was going to say, someone's been questioning "Barbie" ever since--JOSH SCHAFER: The same person that hasn't seen the movie, didn't love the album. But the one thing--ALEXANDRA CANAL: [INAUDIBLE].JOSH SCHAFER: Well, I like the Barbie girl song, the Nicki Minaj song. I think that one's good. I've heard that one on TikTok.ALEXANDRA CANAL: That's surprising.[INTERPOSING VOICES]JOSH SCHAFER: But I did you bring a trivia question, too, because I was curious about this. What do you guys think the most downloaded or I guess bought? Because it's going back to before we downloaded albums from a movie is, the most downloaded movie soundtrack, most purchased movie soundtrack. Any ideas?Story continuesALEXANDRA CANAL: I have no idea. I know like "Armageddon" makes me think of--SEANA SMITH: "Armageddon" is a good one.JOSH SCHAFER: Whitney Houston's "The Bodyguard." Because do you know what song was the headline of that?SEANA SMITH: One that got 45 million copies that were sold.JOSH SCHAFER: "I will Always Love You," Whitney Houston sings in that movie. But it did sort of remind me of what I like more about some movie soundtracks, which is when you have a very talented musical person, it makes for a really fun soundtrack, because you get a bunch of originals out of it. Think like "A Star is Born" with Lady Gaga. I really like that soundtrack more. That was the thing I didn't love about the "Barbie" soundtrack. There's a Ryan Gosling song on there, but it's not that good.SEANA SMITH: Yeah, but--JOSH SCHAFER: Like the actors weren't singers. So it's fun when the actors--SEANA SMITH: Ryan Gosling was a singer when he was younger.JOSH SCHAFER: He's not-- he's not Lady Gaga. He's not Lady Gaga.ALEXANDRA CANAL: No, but he was cute and funny. And that was the whole point of the movie, being cute.JOSH SCHAFER: Well, I haven't seen the movie. So I'm basing it off not seeing the movie.SEANA SMITH: But I think it also just speaks right to the fact that movies here can just play such a massive impact on the music industry in terms of sales, in terms of resurrecting some of those older songs, like you just said with Matchbox Twenty, and really even finding new stars. We've seen that happen time and time again with releases that have happened in the past and what that could mean for artists going forward.I have also not seen the movie yet. But I've heard a lot of these songs. A lot of them I've discovered via TikTok. So here we are in 2023 with the massive success, obviously, of TikTok. So many people finding these trends on that. And I think that also just unlocks future gains here for the music industry and movie tie-ups.JOSH SCHAFER: It gets to the music trend that we've talked about a lot, right, with the fact that you hear it now on TikTok. You and I both haven't even seen the movie, and I knew half the songs because I like, I could see them on TikTok. Right.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Right. I mean, I just remember "Dreams" a with the cranberry juice phenomenon. I'm a big Fleetwood Mac fan. And the fact that people are calling it that TikTok song really got me. But, hey, if that exposes it to a new generation, I'm all for it.SEANA SMITH: There we go. All right. Guys, we got to leave that there.]

Title: 'Equalizer 3' claims top box office spot over Labor Day Weekend
Text: [The third installment in Denzel Washington's Equalizer franchise took the top box office spot over the holiday weekend. Yahoo Finance Entertainment Reporter Alexandra Canal details the summer box office revenue after the premieres of the Barbie movie and Oppenheimer, while also commenting on Disney's (DIS) push to have streaming customers subscribe to Hulu's live-TV package.Video Transcript- Denzel Washington has made a return to the top spot at the box office this holiday weekend with the third installment of Equalizer, which is expected to wrap up the four day weekend at $42 million. That's according to Comscore. Now Barbie took the second spot with Blue Beetle, Gran Turismo, and Oppenheimer rounding out the top five. Yahoo Finance's Alexandra Canal joins us now with the details. Hey, Allie.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Hi, Rachelle. Yes. A solid Labor Day weekend at the box office, thanks in large part to the Equalizer 3. And Labor Day weekend, it hasn't historically been a holiday that draws people out to the theater. But this year seems to be a noteworthy exception. The film made $34.5 million in its opening weekend. And as you mentioned, is estimated to pull in 42 million over the four-day holiday weekend.And if we compare that to years past, that makes this year the second highest Labor Day weekend ever behind 2021. And remember, in 2021, we saw the debut of Marvel's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, which pulled in just under $100 million in that opening two years ago. So still a very strong start here, especially considering we don't have a Marvel film to save the box office this time around.And it's interesting to see the different types of movies that are outperforming at the box office this year. Obviously, The Equalizer. Huge star attached to that with Denzel Washington. An action movie. Typically, those are the movies that do well at the theater. However, this year, we're seeing different types of films emerge, like Barbie starring Margot Robbie. That was a huge success this summer. In fact, as the summer comes to a close the box office revenue hit $4 billion for the first time since the pandemic. So that's a huge win moving forward.Story continuesI will say there are certainly risks heading into the back half of this year. For example, Warner Brothers' Dune 2. That was pushed from November of this year to March of next year. And that was one of the most anticipated films of the fall. And the fact that we don't have that much content heading in to the back half of 2023 is concerning, especially amid these ongoing strikes in Hollywood. Dune 2 was pushed because of the strikes, and we could see potentially more reshuffling of the box office calendar as we head into the end of the year.So a lot to keep track of here, and certainly, the strikes are going to continue to have an impact. But so far at the box office, we're still seeing people come out to the theater, which is encouraging.- It's true. And even with a big name. I mean, look at Indiana Jones, that didn't do well. So I mean, it's kind of hit and miss for some of these as well. I also want to shift gears and look at the streaming space. Disney making a move to push users to subscribe to Hulu and its live TV offerings. What can you tell us there? That does seem like a like a reversal of fortunes here.ALEXANDRA CANAL: Yeah. So this follows the dispute that we saw late last week with Charter Communications, which is the parent company of Spectrum and Disney. If you remember last week, we had a lot of angry sports fans who were unable to watch the US Open, unable to watch college football. After Disney and Charter failed to reach an agreement, Disney then pulled all of its owned and operated channels from subscribers of Charter. So you weren't able to watch ABC, ESPN, even the Disney Channel. So that was very disappointing to those users.But now, Disney has an interesting tactic this morning, saying, if you're a subscriber to Charter and you're disappointed with all these blackouts, why don't you go and subscribe to Hulu Plus Live TV? So that's an interesting move to try and pump your own streaming offerings there. But we've heard from a lot of analysts that say Charter might be OK at the end of the day with this if a dispute is not resolved. However, this could have larger implications to the larger media space considering companies like Disney, Warner Brothers, Discovery, Paramount Global, they depend very heavily on the cash flow from linear networks.So if this sets a precedent moving forward, that could be devastating down the line. So this is something we're continuing to track and watch very closely since this feud, it's still ongoing at the moment.- We'll certainly be keeping track of that. It certainly does put front of mind all the streaming services available and just how much we're spending on them and then the streaming live TV options. It's a lot for us to have to deal with at the moment. But I know you'll keep us up to speed on all of it. Thank you so much, our very own Allie Canal.]

Mattel CEO on Barbie movie: Here's how much we will make from the blockbuster in 2023
Text: [Mattel's (MAT) financial haul from the juggernaut Barbie movie is not all fun and games.It's real money — and a lot of it.Gross billings from Barbie, which include Mattel's cut of the movie box office and various merchandise, will be more than $125 million this year, Mattel chairman and CEO Ynon Kreiz told Yahoo Finance Live (video above) at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Tech Conference in San Francisco.The operating margin from these sales will be above a meaty 60%."It is more than we assumed entering the year, and we expect that in future years there will be continued benefit from the movie," Kreiz said.Mattel and Warner Bros. Title: 'Barbie' movie: Mattel's gross billings to rise by $125M thanks to film, CEO says
Text: [Barbie has dominated the summer box office grossing over $1.4B worldwide. One of the big beneficiaries has been the company that makes the toy, Mattel (MAT). Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz sat down with Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi to discuss all things Barbie, Mattel, and how the company has shifted in it's approach. According to Kreiz, gross billings, as a direct result of the Barbie movie, will increase by $125 million, at about a 60% operating income margin.Bigger picture, Kreiz explains the company's approach in “long-term franchise management” and how the company evolved from a toy manufacturing company to “an IP company that manages franchises”, using “cultural events to benefit the company for years to come." "It's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engage with your fans across multiple levels," Kreiz zays, adding that the opportunities are beyond just films.Click here for more of Yahoo Finance's coverage from the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference.Video TranscriptBRIAN SOZZI: Mattel chairman and CEO Ynon Kreiz. Ynon, where's-- Will Ferrell's behind you somewhere, right? I'm looking for him, no?YNON KREIZ: Great to see you, Brian. Thank you for having me.BRIAN SOZZI: So what is next on the Barbie front? We're starting to see every week the gross theater receipts continue to increase. You're approaching $2 billion. What is next for this franchise?YNON KREIZ: Well, we couldn't be more excited about the way the movie played out to resounding success, a real execution of Greta Gerwig's vision. And what we're seeing coming out of it, three things. It's the strength and cultural resonance of our brands, is our ability to attract, collaborate, and partner with top creative talent, and our ability to promote and create a cultural event of this movie, leveraging our commercial capabilities in partnership with Warner Brothers, who did a terrific job marketing the movie. So it's been a real combination driven by strong brand and great execution, both creatively and commercially.Story continuesBRIAN SOZZI: Your CFO gave a presentation earlier this morning, I think, for the first time, shared some numbers on how much Mattel may make from this movie. Can you share some of those numbers? And what does it mean for the future financial performance of the company?YNON KREIZ: Yes, we did talk about our revenue, gross billing this year to go up by about $125 million from movie, direct movie participation, toys, and consumer products directly related to the movie, not other Barbie product, at a 60%-- sorry, yeah, 60% operating income margin. So about $75 million operating income contribution directly related to the movie in 2023.BRIAN SOZZI: Is that higher than your expectations? Because from an outside looking in, that's a huge number. And in many respects, Ynon, that's a number that you didn't have last year on the financial statements.YNON KREIZ: Well, we did not expect the movie to be as successful. So it is more than we assumed entering the year. And we expect that in future years, there will be continued benefit from the movie. This is about long-term franchise management. It's not just about the quarter or the year.And we-- it's the thing that we've always talked about, you and me. This was the approach. It was never about just trying to sell more toys. It was about creating a cultural event, creating a societal moment. And we believe the benefit will carry forward for years to come.BRIAN SOZZI: We've talked a lot throughout the years. And this is the first time I've heard you mention franchise management. What does that mean as it pertains to now this cultural juggernaut that you've created? Of course, the Barbie brand has been there for decades. But now you have the movie, you have the content component. How do you manage this?YNON KREIZ: We started our journey as a toy company, as a toy manufacturing company. We evolved to be an IP company that manages franchises. And the biggest change in how we approach our business is to realize that people who buy our products and not just consumers, they are fans. And once you have a lot of fans, it's an audience.And when you realize that you have an audience, it changes the conversation. And the opportunity for you to continue to grow your business. And given that we own one of the strongest portfolios in children and family entertainment franchises in the world, this creates a very unique and exciting opportunities-- opportunity for us to grow outside of the toy aisle into highly accretive business verticals driven by big brands and big franchises, which we own. And the "Barbie" movie, we look-- we see as a template, as an example, in terms of how we approach franchise management and expect more to come.BRIAN SOZZI: You have a portfolio of really amazing toy brands that all of us in many respects have grown up using. How do you take this playbook and apply it to some of these brands? What will we see from Mattel over the next 24 months?YNON KREIZ: Our brands are very much timely as much as they are timeless. And we've been doing a lot of work around infusing cultural relevance and societal awareness for what we do with a very strong purpose behind our brands. So it's more than a toy. What we create is more than a play system. It's a holistic approach to engaging-- engage with your fans across multiple levels.And the opportunity for us is not just film. It's also television. It's video games. It's location-based entertainment. It's musicals. It's-- whatever medium is driven by big franchises and big brands. In today's world, this is what it's all about-- big brands, big franchises that elevate and rise above a crowded marketplace. And we believe we are at the beginning of a very exciting part of our journey.BRIAN SOZZI: Well, it's going to be hard to create another nearly $2 billion movie. It just doesn't happen very often. But within the portfolios that you and the portfolio brands you own, what's the brand you're really focused on that you're going to run this playbook with next?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. We're not saying every movie that we make will be as successful, but it will be the same approach, the same methodology, and the same creative take that we are looking to apply. There's the "Hot Wheels" movie that we're developing with JJ Abrams. There's a Matchbox movie with Skydance, which produced "Mission Impossible" and "Top Gun." There's a movie we're developing with Vin Diesel for Rock'em Sock'em Robots, Polly Pocket with Lena Dunham and Lily Collins, and Major Matt Mason with Tom Hanks written by Akiva Goldsman.So these are just a few examples of some of the projects that we're developing. And you can see, given the quality and strength and proven track record of our partners, we believe we have a real shot at creating exciting projects that will appeal to global audiences. And what we saw within the "Barbie" movie is that the picture appealed not just to the core buyers of Barbie toys, Barbie product, this was a much broader approach to global audiences across different demographics, men and women, different ages, different generations. And everyone found something that talked to them and touch them at an emotional level.And the credit goes to the incredible execution of this project by Greta Gerwig, who had such a vision and, of course, Margot Robbie as a producer and a lead actor, Ryan Gosling, and, of course, the soundtrack that was a key part of the holistic experience, all of it created something very special that we're very proud of.BRIAN SOZZI: This-- this didn't happen overnight. But my sense has been that you saw the potential of this happening many years ago when you took over at Mattel. From a leadership perspective, how did you identify that? And then how do you ultimately go about bringing that to life?YNON KREIZ: Yeah. This journey has been long in the making, started about five years ago. And from the very beginning, the approach was to create something that was not conventional, something that was not traditional. And the term "cultural event" is what we said back in the day. It was never about trying to make a movie or, for that matter, make a movie in order to sell toys.The focus was to create a quality content, quality content that people will want to watch. And we know that if we do that, and if we do that well, good things will happen. And we will sell a lot of toys. So it's not that we didn't want to sell toys, but the mandate and the approach and the relationship and the engagement with the creatives that partnered with us was to focus on making a great movie and not think about selling toys.And what we see now, of course, we have a great movie. We see the success at the box office. And we also are starting to see the success on the toy side of the company with POS for the company year-to-date up, Barbie gaining momentum. And overall, we see good, very exciting opportunity for us to continue to gain share.BRIAN SOZZI: Seemingly, every day, over the past three months, I've read another story about the "Barbie" movie, something new happening. But also, you, you've been front and center in a lot of these stories and on, as you should be, because you brought this to life, this cultural event. How have you stayed grounded? And how do you look-- how are you looking to stay grounded over the next few months when you have all these publications writing about you, telling you how successful you are? And how do you just stay focused with all this frenzy around yourself?YNON KREIZ: Well, this very much has been a team effort. It's been a journey with a lot of people that participated and made it all happen. And I couldn't be more proud of the team and everything that we've done collectively. For this to be successful, for this movie to be where it is today, it took a lot of effort. And I'm grateful for everyone's support and involvement.And we really do see it as a beginning of a new chapter. This is not a one-off movie. It's not a one-off project. This has been the strategy. And you followed our story, and you know that we've been consistently made progress in building and driving our IP strategy to reach this point.But it's not the moment we've been waiting to arrive, and we're done by any stretch. This is really one-- another step in the journey. We see it as a template. We see it as an example. As I said before, this is the approach. And we look to replicate that approach in terms of leveraging our brands that have been foundational in this case specifically-- you know, Barbie, it's the "Barbie" movie-- working with top talent that have a clear vision and are the best in what they do, which we have done in this movie as well. And of course, commercializing and executing the marketing level and creating demand in a marketplace that became a cultural phenomenon. And so this has been a great and exciting journey. And we're still very much at the early stage of it.BRIAN SOZZI: Thanks for making a little time for little old me and on. I appreciate it. I know you're the big star now. But I appreciate it. Thanks for always giving time to Yahoo Finance. It's been fun to follow this journey. I mean, hat tip to you and your team. Ynon Kreiz, Chairman and CEO of Mattel.Seana, back to you in New York. I know you're a big fan of the "Barbie" movie.SEANA SMITH: I am a big fan of the "Barbie" movie. We've been talking about it for over a year. So, of course, our thanks to you, saw all the great interviews out there, and Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz as well.]
